narrative:
The model predicted a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Placing in the bottom decile of your class, compared with an average around the middle of the pack among accepted students, signaled to the model a high risk of struggling with the bar. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; you stood in the second decile while successful applicants averaged near the sixth.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential feature, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 2.5 it is below the 3.23 average of accepted students, yet the model still treated the value itself as mildly encouraging because even this modest GPA was not low enough to outweigh the other signals.

Taken together, the model concluded that your relatively low class standings created too great a likelihood of bar exam failure. To strengthen future applications, you should focus on raising your academic performance, particularly your class rank in later years, or consider programs that offer additional bar-preparation support before reapplying.
